title: The Trinity
summary: From the Nicene homoousios to the Council of Florence: one God in three persons, each fully God, distinct only by their relations of origin.

steps.note: Nicaea: the Son is of one substance with the Father, against Arius.
Constantinople I: the Holy Spirit is Lord and giver of life, adored and glorified with the Father and the Son.
Damasus's synod: the Holy Spirit is truly God, of the divine substance, like the Son.
The Athanasian Creed: unity in Trinity and Trinity in unity, persons not confused, substance not divided.
Toledo XI: a full Latin confession of the Trinity, persons distinguished by relation.
Lateran IV: one supreme reality, Father, Son and Spirit; against Joachim's account of the divine unity (n. 431).
Lyons II: the Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son as from one principle.
Florence: the Greek "through the Son" means the same faith as the Latin "and the Son."
Florence, for the Jacobites: in God all is one except where there is opposition of relation.
Leo XIV marks 1700 years of Nicaea and presents its faith as the ground of Christian unity.

title: Christ, true God and true man
summary: The councils from Ephesus to Constantinople III fix the confession of one person in two natures with two wills, and later ecumenical agreements measure other traditions by it.

steps.note: Ephesus receives Cyril's letter: the Word united flesh to himself hypostatically.
Ephesus: Mary is Mother of God, because the one she bore is God the Word made flesh.
Leo's Tome: each nature keeps its properties, joined in one person.
Chalcedon: one and the same Christ in two natures, without confusion, change, division or separation.
Constantinople II: Cyril's "one nature of the Word made flesh" is accepted only in the Fathers' sense.
Honorius writes ambiguously of one will (the case later debated, see the disputed questions).
Constantinople III: two natural wills and two operations, the human will following the divine.
Lateran IV: the Son incarnate by the whole Trinity, true God and true man.
1994: the Assyrian Church of the East and Rome confess the same faith under different titles for Mary.

title: Mary
summary: From Mother of God to the Assumption, with the Immaculate Conception moving from permitted opinion to dogma, and titles of mediation left undefined.

steps.note: Ephesus: Theotokos, Mother of God, defended against Nestorius.
Siricius: Mary's virginity after the birth of Christ.
Lateran Synod of 649: Mary ever-virgin, conceiving without seed and giving birth without corruption.
Sixtus IV approves a feast of the Immaculate Conception while the question is still debated.
Sixtus IV forbids each side to call the other heretical.
Trent declines to include Mary in its decree on original sin.
Alexander VII describes the belief in her preservation from original sin from the first instant.
Pius IX defines the Immaculate Conception (1854).
Leo XIII: Mary as mediatrix to the Mediator, in a subordinate sense.
Pius XII defines the Assumption (1950), the last dogma defined.
Lumen Gentium 8 places Mary within the mystery of Christ and the Church.
2025: Co-redemptrix judged inappropriate; Mary's subordinate cooperation reaffirmed.

title: Primacy and infallibility of the Pope
summary: From Clement's letter to Corinth to Vatican I's definitions, and the post-conciliar discussion of how the primacy is exercised.

steps.note: Clement of Rome intervenes in the church of Corinth.
Serdica: bishops may appeal to the bishop of Rome.
Siricius: Peter bears the burdens of all in his successor.
Innocent I: matters from all provinces are referred to the Apostolic See.
Boniface I: what Rome has decided may not be reopened.
At Ephesus the papal legate: Peter lives and judges in his successors.
Unam Sanctam: subjection to the Roman Pontiff is necessary for salvation.
Constance, amid three rival claimants, asserts authority over anyone "even if papal" (Haec Sancta); its standing is disputed.
Florence: the Pope has primacy over the whole world and full power to rule the Church.
Florence condemns Basel's claim that a council's superiority over the pope is a truth of faith.
Pius II forbids appeals from the pope to a future council.
Lateran V: the pope alone convokes, transfers and dissolves councils.
Vatican I: the primacy of jurisdiction is immediate and episcopal over all the faithful.
Vatican I: the Pope's power is full and supreme, not merely supervision.
Vatican I defines papal infallibility and its conditions.
Lumen Gentium repeats Vatican I and sets collegiality under and with the head.
John Paul II invites discussion of the exercise, not the substance, of the primacy.

title: Scripture and Tradition
summary: The canon, the two channels of revelation, inspiration and inerrancy, and the Church's authority to interpret.

steps.note: Damasus's council lists the canon of Scripture.
Carthage gives the same canon.
Trent: the Gospel comes in written books and unwritten traditions, both received with equal reverence; the canon fixed.
Trent: no one may interpret Scripture against the Church's sense or the consent of the Fathers.
Vatican I: the books are sacred because written under the Spirit's inspiration with God as author.
Leo XIII: inspiration excludes error from the whole of Scripture.
Pius X requires obedience to the Biblical Commission's decisions.
Benedict XV rejects limiting inerrancy to religious matters.
Pius XII: the interpreter must attend to the literary forms of the ancient writers.
Dei Verbum restates the doctrine and speaks of the truth recorded for our salvation.

title: Grace and justification
summary: From the African councils against Pelagius to Trent's decree, the Jansenist condemnations, and the Joint Declaration with Lutherans.

steps.note: Carthage: grace helps us not to sin, not only forgives past sins.
Carthage: without grace we can do nothing, not merely do good with more difficulty.
The Indiculus: God is the author of every good disposition, and free choice is set free, not destroyed.
Orange II: free will weakened in Adam is repaired only by the grace of baptism.
Trent: the beginning of justification is from prevenient grace, with free cooperation.
Trent's canons on justification, from the first against Pelagianism to the last against misreadings of the decree.
Paul V: Thomists and Molinists may each teach their view on efficacious grace.
Innocent X condemns Jansen's first proposition: some commandments impossible to the just.
Clement XI condemns Quesnel's claim that no grace is given outside the Church.
1999: Catholics and Lutherans state a consensus on basic truths of justification.

title: Original sin and the unity of the human race
summary: The doctrine defended against Pelagius, defined at Trent, and kept as the fixed point in modern questions about evolution and unbaptized infants.

steps.note: Carthage: Adam was not made subject to death by nature but by sin.
Carthage: infants are baptized for the remission of sin they contract from Adam.
Orange II: Adam's sin passed death and sin to the whole human race.
Trent: Adam's transgression harmed his posterity, transmitting sin and death.
Trent: newborn infants are to be baptized for the remission of original sin.
Pius VI rejects calling limbo a Pelagian fable.
Pius XII permits research on the evolution of the human body.
Pius XII: polygenism cannot be held while it is not apparent how it fits original sin.
2007: a theological study on hope for unbaptized infants.

title: The Eucharist
summary: Real presence, transubstantiation and sacrifice, from Berengarius to Trent and Paul VI.

steps.note: Berengarius's oath: bread and wine are substantially changed into Christ's body and blood.
Lateran IV: the bread and wine are transubstantiated.
Constance condemns Wycliffe's claim that the substance of bread remains.
Constance defends communion under one kind for the laity.
Trent: Christ is truly, really and substantially contained under the species.
Trent: the change is fittingly and properly called transubstantiation.
Trent: the Church may change how sacraments are administered, preserving their substance.
Trent: the Mass is a true and proper sacrifice.
The Holy Office judges a proposed philosophical account of transubstantiation intolerable.
Paul VI reaffirms transubstantiation against theories of mere change of meaning.
The revised Missal changes the rites, not the doctrine of the Mass.

title: Penance and confession
summary: From private confession under Leo the Great to the annual precept and Trent's canons, and reconciliation of the dying.

steps.note: Innocent I: penance and communion for the dying.
Celestine I: penance must not be refused to the dying who ask for it.
Leo the Great: secret confession to priests suffices; public reading of sins is forbidden.
Lateran IV: every Catholic confesses at least once a year.
Florence: the matter and form of penance.
Trent: confession of all mortal sins is of divine law.
Trent: penance is truly and properly a sacrament.
Trent: sacramental confession is instituted by divine law and necessary for salvation.
Paul VI reorganizes penitential practice while keeping the duty of penance.

title: Marriage
summary: Indissolubility, sacramentality and the ends of marriage, and the post-conciliar questions about Communion and blessings.

steps.note: Elvira: a woman who leaves an adulterous husband may not remarry while he lives.
Innocent III's profession for the Waldensians affirms that marriage is lawful and good.
Florence: marriage is the seventh sacrament, sign of Christ and the Church.
Trent: the Church does not err in teaching that adultery does not dissolve the bond.
Leo XIII, Arcanum: the Church's authority over Christian marriage.
Pius XI, Casti Connubii: marriage instituted and restored by God, not by man.
Casti Connubii: any use of marriage deliberately frustrated of its power to procreate is grave sin.
Casti Connubii against divorce.
Humanae Vitae repeats the teaching on contraception.
Familiaris Consortio 84 on the divorced and remarried.
Amoris Laetitia, chapter 8, and the dispute over its reading.
Fiducia Supplicans: blessings of persons, with the doctrine of marriage restated.

title: The Church and salvation
summary: From Pelagius II and Lateran IV to Florence, Pius IX on invincible ignorance, and Vatican II's teaching on the Church.

steps.note: Pelagius II: one slain outside the Church cannot attain its rewards.
Innocent III's profession: the one Church outside which no one is saved.
Lateran IV: one universal Church of the faithful, outside which no one at all is saved.
Unam Sanctam: subjection to the Roman Pontiff necessary for salvation.
Florence: those outside the Church cannot share eternal life unless joined to it before death.
Trent: justification requires baptism or the desire for it.
Clement XI condemns the claim that no grace is given outside the Church.
Pius IX: outside the Church no salvation, and invincible ignorance is no fault before God.
Pius IX: those in invincible ignorance who keep the natural law can attain eternal life by grace.
Pius XII, Mystici Corporis: who are members of the Church.
Lumen Gentium 8 and 14-16.
Dominus Iesus: Christ the one Savior, the Church necessary.

title: Church, state and religious liberty
summary: From the two swords to Leo XIII's Christian state, Pius IX's condemnations, and Dignitatis Humanae.

steps.note: Unam Sanctam: the two swords, temporal and spiritual.
Pius IX, Quanta Cura: liberty of conscience and worship as a right of every man condemned.
Syllabus 15: the claim that each is free to embrace any religion reason judges true, condemned.
Syllabus 77: the claim that the Catholic religion should no longer be the religion of the state, condemned.
Leo XIII, Immortale Dei: two powers, each supreme in its sphere.
Leo XIII: rulers may tolerate other worships for a great good or to avoid evil.
Dignitatis Humanae: civil immunity from coercion, with the duty toward the true religion untouched.
Benedict XVI on this case as reform in continuity.

title: Death, judgment, heaven, hell and purgatory
summary: From the condemnation of universal restoration to Benedictus Deus and Trent on purgatory.

steps.note: Against Origenism: the punishment of the damned does not end.
Innocent IV: those who die unrepentant in mortal sin suffer forever.
Lyons II: purgatory, the immediate vision for the purified, and hell for those in mortal sin.
Benedict XII defines the immediate beatific vision for the purified.
Benedict XII: those who die in mortal sin descend immediately to hell.
Florence: the purified are received into heaven; those in mortal or original sin alone go to hell with unequal punishments.
Trent: there is a purgatory, and souls there are helped by the prayers of the faithful.
Pius VI on limbo.
2007: hope for unbaptized infants.

title: Faith and reason
summary: Nineteenth-century debates over rationalism and fideism, settled at Vatican I and restated against Modernism.

steps.note: Propositions Bautain was required to sign: reason can prove God's existence, against fideism.
Pius IX, Qui pluribus: faith and reason do not conflict.
Vatican I: God can be known with certainty by the natural light of reason.
Vatican I: faith is assent to God revealing, on his authority.
Vatican I: two orders of knowledge, distinct in principle and object.
Vatican I: there can never be real disagreement between faith and reason.
The Oath against Modernism: God can be known and proved by reason.
Pius XII, Humani Generis: errors threatening the foundations of doctrine.
Donum Veritatis on the vocation of the theologian.

title: Development of doctrine
summary: How dogma can grow in understanding without changing its meaning: the key principle of the hermeneutic of continuity.

steps.note: Gelasius: what has once been condemned is not to be reopened.
Vatican I: the understanding of dogma grows, but in the same doctrine, the same sense, the same meaning.
Vatican I: anathema to anyone who says dogmas may take a sense other than the Church's.
Lamentabili 54 condemns the claim that dogmas and sacraments evolve as mere interpretations.
Lamentabili 58: truth is not mutable with man.
Pascendi on the Modernist theory that dogma must evolve and change.
The Oath against Modernism rejects the evolution of dogma from one meaning to another.
Mysterium Ecclesiae: formulas are historically conditioned, but their meaning remains true.
Benedict XVI's hermeneutic of reform in continuity.

title: The dignity of human life
summary: Abortion, the killing of the innocent and the death penalty, from the medieval professions to Evangelium Vitae and the 2018 revision.

steps.note: Innocent III: civil power may impose the death penalty without mortal sin.
Innocent XI condemns permitting abortion before animation.
Innocent XI condemns the claim that the fetus probably lacks a rational soul until birth.
Holy Office: any operation directly killing the fetus or the mother cannot be safely taught.
Pius XI, Casti Connubii: the killing of the unborn.
Pius XII on artificial fertilization.
1974: abortion gravely wrong from conception, ensoulment left open.
Evangelium Vitae's three solemn confirmations.
2018: the death penalty called inadmissible; read in continuity with n. 425.
Dignitas Infinita on grave violations of human dignity.

title: Property, work and the social order
summary: From the condemnation of usury to the social encyclicals of Leo XIII and Pius XI, and their successors.

steps.note: Lateran II condemns usurers.
Lateran V approves the Mountains of Piety and their modest charges.
Benedict XIV, Vix pervenit: profit from a loan by reason of the loan itself is usury.
Leo XIII, Rerum Novarum: the natural right to private property and a just wage.
Pius XI, Quadragesimo Anno: the Church's authority in social and economic questions.
Pius XI: property has an individual and a social character.
Pius XI: socialism cannot be reconciled with Catholic teaching.
Gaudium et Spes on economic and social life.
Laudato Si' on the universal destination of goods and creation.
Leo XIV on love for the poor.

title: Holy orders and ministry
summary: The grades of orders, the matter and form of ordination, Anglican orders, and post-conciliar changes in ministry.

steps.note: Elvira: continence required of bishops, priests and deacons.
Trent: there are several orders, major and minor, ordered to the priesthood.
Trent: other orders besides the priesthood exist in the Church.
Leo XIII judges Anglican orders invalid.
Pius XII fixes the matter and form of ordination.
Paul VI suppresses the minor orders and the subdiaconate.
1976: the reasons for reserving priesthood to men.
1994: the reservation declared to be held definitively.
2009: married former Anglican clergy ordained Catholic priests.
2025: the commission on women deacons, not definitive.
